title: Twice-Cooked Pork
subtitle: poached pork belly slices stir-fried with leeks and doubanjiang
excerpt: Pork belly is first simmered until just cooked, then sliced thin and returned to a very hot wok with leeks and a spicy, fermented sauce. The double cooking gives the pork a blistered, slightly crisped edge. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Hui guo rou (twice-cooked pork) is one of the most iconic dishes in Sichuan cooking, documented in detail in Fuchsia Dunlop's 'Land of Plenty' (2001) and traced to Sichuan culinary texts compiled by the Sichuan Higher Institute of Cuisine in the 1970s and 1980s. The technique of poaching pork then stir-frying it is found across Chinese provincial cuisines, but the Sichuan version with doubanjiang and sweet fermented sauce is the most celebrated.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Poach the pork belly up to a day ahead, slice, and refrigerate. Stir-fry from cold when ready to serve.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fermented paste made from broad beans and chillies, central to Sichuan cooking. It is salty, spicy and deeply savoury. Pixian county doubanjiang is considered the finest variety.

A fatty, layered cut from the underside of the pig with alternating bands of meat and fat. When briefly poached then stir-fried, the fat renders and the edges char slightly, creating a rich texture that pairs well with robust sauces.
A Chinese rice wine with a nutty, amber flavour used widely in marinades, sauces and braises. Named after the city of Shaoxing in Zhejiang province. Dry sherry is the closest substitute.

Literally 'breath of the wok'. The slightly smoky, charred aroma that develops when food is cooked over very high heat in a well-seasoned wok. Achieved at home by getting the wok as hot as possible before adding oil.

content.text: Twice-cooked pork takes about 50 minutes and serves 4.
Pork belly
is simmered in seasoned water until just cooked through, then sliced and returned to a searingly hot wok with leeks and
doubanjiang
. A splash of
Shaoxing wine
and a final blast of high heat to get some
wok hei
finish the dish.
Chill the belly briefly after poaching before slicing. Cold meat cuts into clean, even slices far more easily than warm.
What you need

items.prepNote: white and light green parts, cut into 4 cm pieces

content.text: Method
Put the pork belly in a pot, cover with cold water, add the sliced ginger and 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine. Bring to the boil, reduce to a simmer and cook for 25 minutes.
Remove the pork and rest for 10 minutes. Slice thinly, about 3 mm thick, across the grain.
Heat the wok over high heat until smoking. Add the oil and lay in the pork slices in a single layer. Fry for 2 minutes without stirring until the fat starts to render and the edges char slightly.
Push the pork to the side. Add the doubanjiang and fry for 30 seconds until the oil turns red.
Add the garlic and stir everything together. Cook for 30 seconds.
Add the leeks and toss for 2 minutes until softened but still with some bite.
Pour in the remaining 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine, the dark soy sauce and sugar. Toss everything for 1 minute over high heat.
Serve immediately with steamed rice.

items.cause: The belly was sliced too thick or undercooked during poaching.
items.fix: Simmer for a full 25 minutes and slice no thicker than 3 mm. Thinner slices also fry faster in the wok.

items.cause: Too little time in the wok.
items.fix: Cook the leeks for at least 2 minutes, tossing continuously. They should be soft with some green colour remaining.

items.cause: Doubanjiang and dark soy together can overload the seasoning.
items.fix: Use only 1 tbsp doubanjiang and taste before adding the soy sauce.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Twice-cooked pork is a Sichuan classic and one of the most ordered dishes in Sichuan restaurants both inside and outside China. The double-cooking method, poaching followed by stir-frying, produces a texture that is hard to get any other way: the fat is almost translucent, the edges are lightly charred and the sauce clings to every slice. Garlic shoots are the traditional vegetable in Sichuan; leeks are a common and easy substitute.
